# Three.js Air Conditioning Understanding

## Objective

Create a premium interactive 3D experience that helps anyone understand how reversible air conditioning moves heat.

The experience must clearly compare:

- a split system with an indoor unit and an outdoor unit connected by refrigerant lines;
- a monoblock system containing the complete refrigeration circuit in one indoor cabinet with separate outdoor intake and exhaust airflow;
- Cooling mode and Heating mode for both systems.

## What the user should understand

After using the experience, a first-time viewer should understand that air conditioning moves heat rather than creating cold, that refrigerant travels in a sealed loop, that indoor and outdoor air remain separate, and that Heating mode reverses the roles of the two heat exchangers.

Show the important HVAC elements clearly: heat exchangers, compressor, expansion device, reversing valve, fans, refrigerant lines, airflow, heat transfer, and condensation where relevant. Use animated particles and a clear legend to distinguish room air, outdoor air, refrigerant, and heat energy.

## Experience requirements

- Use Three.js to create a realistic cutaway scene centered on one wall separating a believable interior from the outdoors.
- Provide controls for Split System / Monoblock and Cooling / Heating.
- Include orbit and zoom controls, Play / Pause, Reset View, and a short replayable guided explanation.
- Use concise labels and small synchronized tutorial messages that explain what is happening without covering the scene.
- Show the current system state, indoor and outdoor temperatures, and where heat is absorbed and released.
- Every visible control must work on desktop and mobile.
- Use the model name as the browser title and the primary visible title, with no additional title text.

## Quality bar

Prioritize exceptional visual quality and realism. The result should feel like a high-end interactive museum exhibit or a premium engineering visualization.

Use convincing proportions, detailed components, physically suggestive materials, refined lighting, shadows, depth, smooth animation, realistic airflow, elegant particles, clean callouts, strong composition, and a sophisticated interface. The scene must remain easy to read while looking cinematic and professionally art-directed.

Choose the visual direction, layout, camera composition, geometry, materials, animation system, and tutorial presentation yourself. Do not follow a prescribed implementation path. Focus on the strongest finished result.

## Technical constraints

- Deliver one self-contained standalone HTML application.
- Load Three.js and official Three.js helpers from a CDN.
- Do not use external images, textures, videos, fonts, APIs, or 3D model files.
- Use procedural geometry and materials.
- Handle resizing, high-DPI screens, reduced motion, and WebGL failure gracefully.
- The application must open directly in a modern browser without a build step.

## Execution discipline

Choose one strong design direction and implement it once. After implementation, perform one concise validation pass covering page load and the essential controls, fix only a blocking error found by that pass, and then stop.

Do not run repeated browser or screenshot review loops. Do not repeatedly redesign, rewrite, polish, or auto-correct the application after it is functional. Do not spend time iterating against your own screenshots. Avoid open-ended self-critique cycles.

Build the experience directly without first explaining your design. Keep the final response brief.

Work only inside the current working directory. Do not read, list, search, or edit files outside the current working directory. Treat it as a standalone project root.

Use pnpm exclusively if dependency installation or package scripts are needed. Do not use npm.
Set the browser title and the primary visible title to your model name, using only identity information already available to you. Add nothing else to either title.
Run the relevant checks yourself. Do not edit files outside the current working directory.

OVERVIEW: Control Portly, the macOS dev server manager.

Portly keeps local dev servers running on fixed ports, restarts them when they
crash, and exposes everything through this CLI so an agent can drive it.

Every command starts Portly.app if it is not already running.

USAGE: portly <subcommand>

OPTIONS:
  --version               Show the version.
  -h, --help              Show help information.

SUBCOMMANDS:
  status, list, ls (default)
                          Show active servers and problems compactly.
  start                   Start a server, or a whole project.
  stop                    Stop a server, a project, or everything.
  restart                 Restart a server or a project.
  action                  Run a configured server action without restarting the
                          server.
  logs                    Print the recent output of a server.
  temp, temporary, run-temp
                          Run a short-lived process without creating a project.
  wait                    Wait for a temporary job and return its exit code.
  add-project             Register a project folder.
  add-server              Add a server to a project.
  update-server           Change an existing server's settings.
  memory-limit, ram-limit Show or configure automatic project restarts by
                          memory footprint.
  remove                  Remove a server or a project.
  take-over, adopt        Stop an external listener and relaunch the configured
                          server under Portly.
  port                    Show what is listening on a port.
  kill-port               Send SIGTERM to whatever holds a port.
  open                    Bring the Portly window to the front.
  quit                    Quit Portly, stopping every server.
  forever                 Keep Portly available across macOS logins.
  config                  Print the config file path and contents.

  See 'portly help <subcommand>' for detailed help.

OVERVIEW: Change an existing server's settings.

USAGE: portly update-server <server> [--name <name>] [--command <command>] [--port <port>] [--directory <directory>] [--health-url <health-url>] [--action <action> ...] [--clear-actions] [--auto-restart] [--no-auto-restart] [--json] [--api-port <api-port>]

ARGUMENTS:
  <server>                Server name or id.

OPTIONS:
  --name <name>
  --command <command>
  --port <port>
  --directory <directory>
  --health-url <health-url>
  --action <action>       Replace maintenance actions with NAME=COMMAND values.
  --clear-actions         Remove every configured action.
  --auto-restart/--no-auto-restart
                          Restart automatically after a crash.
  --json                  Print raw JSON instead of a human summary.
  --api-port <api-port>   Override the control API port.
  --version               Show the version.
  -h, --help              Show help information.

OVERVIEW: Register a project folder.

USAGE: portly add-project --name <name> --path <path> [--icon <icon>] [--color <color>] [--memory-limit <memory-limit>] [--json] [--api-port <api-port>]

OPTIONS:
  --name <name>           Project name.
  --path <path>           Absolute path to the project folder.
  --icon <icon>           SF Symbol name shown in the sidebar, for example
                          globe.
  --color <color>         Hex color for the project icon.
  --memory-limit <memory-limit>
                          Project memory policy: inherit, off, or a size such
                          as 5GB.
  --json                  Print raw JSON instead of a human summary.
  --api-port <api-port>   Override the control API port.
  --version               Show the version.
  -h, --help              Show help information.

content.text:
The app was already fully built in `index.html`, so I only fixed the server, one console error, and two false failures in the validation script.

- **Server:** the Portly server on port 9241 was serving an old copy that had been moved to Trash. I repointed it to this directory, and it now serves the current `index.html`.
- **Console error:** the only page error was a favicon 404. I added an inline `<link rel="icon" href="data:,">`, and the last run showed no console errors.
- **Requirements confirmed:**
  - The browser title and the visible title both read "Claude Sonnet 5.5".
  - The Split/Monoblock and Cooling/Heating controls work, and the state text and temperatures update. I saw about 16 °C indoors and 3 °C outdoors in Heating.
  - Play/Pause works, and the guided tour runs through its steps, closes, and replays.
  - Orbit, Zoom in, Zoom out and Reset View work.
  - The WebGL-failure class was not set on desktop or mobile.
- **False failures in the earlier run:**
  - The full run showed Reset View and desktop Zoom in as failing.
  - That headless software rendering runs at about 1 fps and the app caps each frame's time step, so the camera animations need far more than the 1–2 s the script waited.
  - A re-check with a small viewport that waited for the camera to settle passed for zoom in, zoom out, orbit and reset. Reset returned exactly to the home view.
- **Not verified:** real-GPU frame rate. I did not re-take screenshots.

I left the scratch validation folder `_validate/` (its scripts, `node_modules` and old screenshots) inside the app directory. It's not part of the deliverable and can be deleted.
